claim: FOXP2 expression in the developing cortex is restricted to subpopulations of post-mitotic neurons in the deep cortical layers.
source: FOXP2 expression in the developing cortex is restricted to subpopulations of post-mitotic neurons in the deep cortical layers, a pattern that is highly conserved across mammalian species (Ferland et al., 2003; Takahashi et al., 2003; Campbell et al., 2009; Mukamel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies that have documented this expression pattern.

claim: FOXP2 expression pattern in the developing cortex is highly conserved across mammalian species.
source: FOXP2 expression in the developing cortex is restricted to subpopulations of post-mitotic neurons in the deep cortical layers, a pattern that is highly conserved across mammalian species (Ferland et al., 2003; Takahashi et al., 2003; Campbell et al., 2009; Mukamel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies across multiple mammalian species.

claim: Mutations in FOXP2 cause a severe developmental speech and language disorder, known as childhood apraxia of speech.
source: Mutations in FOXP2 cause a severe developmental speech and language disorder, known as childhood apraxia of speech (Lai et al., 2001; MacDermot et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that identified FOXP2 mutations in patients with childhood apraxia of speech.

claim: FOXP2 protein expression begins between embryonic day (E) 14.5 and E16.5 within postmitotic neurons of the infragranular layers.
source: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry of coronal sections of the embryonic forebrain suggested that FOXP2 protein expression begins between embryonic day (E) 14.5 and E16.5 within postmitotic neurons of the infragranular layers (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Postnatally, Foxp2 expression is limited to glutamatergic neurons of the infragranular cortical layers, with robust expression predominantly in layer 6.
source: Postnatally, it is well established that Foxp2 expression is limited to glutamatergic neurons of the infragranular cortical layers, with robust expression predominantly in layer 6 (Ferland et al., 2003; Hisaoka et al., 2010; Sundberg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Layer 6 is comprised of two primary glutamatergic cortical neuron populations, corticothalamic (CT) and corticocortical (CC) neurons.
source: Layer 6, where most of the FOXP2+ neurons are located, is comprised of two primary glutamatergic cortical neuron populations, corticothalamic (CT) and corticocortical (CC) neurons (Thomson, 2010; Petrof et al., 2012; Harris and Shepherd, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing layer 6 neuron populations.

claim: FOXP2 is expressed in 78.3 ± 2.9% of corticothalamic neurons in layer 6 of primary somatosensory cortex.
source: FOXP2 expression was evident in most CT neurons (Mean ± SEM, 78.3 ± 2.9%), but was expressed by very few CC neurons (Mean ± SEM, 6.4 ± 1.7%; Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: FOXP2 is expressed in only 6.4 ± 1.7% of corticocortical neurons in layer 6 of primary somatosensory cortex.
source: FOXP2 expression was evident in most CT neurons (Mean ± SEM, 78.3 ± 2.9%), but was expressed by very few CC neurons (Mean ± SEM, 6.4 ± 1.7%; Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Nearly all tdTomato-positive Ntsr1-cre neurons in primary somatosensory cortex co-express FOXP2 at P0 (90 ± 2%).
source: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry revealed that nearly all tdTomato-positive neurons in the primary SSC co-expressed FOXP2 at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1F–G, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 90 ± 2%, P7 = 87 ± 2%, P14 = 91 ± 1%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Nearly all tdTomato-positive Ntsr1-cre neurons in primary somatosensory cortex co-express FOXP2 at P7 (87 ± 2%).
source: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry revealed that nearly all tdTomato-positive neurons in the primary SSC co-expressed FOXP2 at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1F–G, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 90 ± 2%, P7 = 87 ± 2%, P14 = 91 ± 1%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Nearly all tdTomato-positive Ntsr1-cre neurons in primary somatosensory cortex co-express FOXP2 at P14 (91 ± 1%).
source: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry revealed that nearly all tdTomato-positive neurons in the primary SSC co-expressed FOXP2 at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1F–G, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 90 ± 2%, P7 = 87 ± 2%, P14 = 91 ± 1%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: MET is expressed in layer 6 corticocortical neurons but nearly excluded from layer 6 corticothalamic neurons in somatosensory cortex.
source: For further molecular characterization, we also examined FOXP2 overlap with the receptor tyrosine kinase MET, which is expressed in CC neurons of layer 6, but nearly excluded from layer 6 CT neurons in SSC (Kast et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Few GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons co-express FOXP2 at P0 (19 ± 2%).
source: Using co-labeling in MetGFP reporter mice (Kast et al., 2019), analysis of FOXP2 expression among GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons revealed relatively few double-positive neurons at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1H–I, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 19 ± 2%, P7 = 16 ± 2%, P14 = 5 ± 2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from MetGFP reporter mice shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Few GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons co-express FOXP2 at P7 (16 ± 2%).
source: Using co-labeling in MetGFP reporter mice (Kast et al., 2019), analysis of FOXP2 expression among GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons revealed relatively few double-positive neurons at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1H–I, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 19 ± 2%, P7 = 16 ± 2%, P14 = 5 ± 2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from MetGFP reporter mice shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Few GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons co-express FOXP2 at P14 (5 ± 2%).
source: Using co-labeling in MetGFP reporter mice (Kast et al., 2019), analysis of FOXP2 expression among GFP+ layer 6 CC neurons revealed relatively few double-positive neurons at P0, P7, and P14 (Figure 1H–I, Mean ± SEM: P0 = 19 ± 2%, P7 = 16 ± 2%, P14 = 5 ± 2%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from MetGFP reporter mice shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: FOXP2 extensively colocalizes with PCP4, a marker of corticothalamic neurons, in layer 6.
source: There was extensive colocalization between FOXP2 and PCP4, a marker of corticothalamic neurons, in layer 6, but there was minimal colocalization between FOXP2 and ppCCK, a marker of CC neurons (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: There is minimal colocalization between FOXP2 and ppCCK, a marker of corticocortical neurons.
source: There was extensive colocalization between FOXP2 and PCP4, a marker of corticothalamic neurons, in layer 6, but there was minimal colocalization between FOXP2 and ppCCK, a marker of CC neurons (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Lower level expression of Foxp2 transcript has been detected in molecularly-defined subcerebral projection neurons by RNA-sequencing at perinatal stages.
source: Notably, lower level expression of Foxp2 transcript has been detected in molecularly-defined subcerebral projection neurons by RNA-sequencing at perinatal stages (Molyneaux et al., 2015), consistent with the low-level expression observed in layer 5 at P0 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an RNA-sequencing study and is consistent with data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FOXP2 is expressed by a minor subset of CTIP2+ pyramidal-tract neurons at P0 (34 ± 3%).
source: However, in contrast to the temporally stable and relatively uniform expression of FOXP2 by CT neurons in layer 6 of the postnatal SSC (Figure 1), FOXP2 was expressed by a minor subset of CTIP2+ PT neurons at P0 (34 ± 3%) and P7 (10 ± 2%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), and was almost completely absent from retrogradely labeled PT neurons in Layer 5 of SSC by P14 (4.4 ± 1.7%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: FOXP2 is expressed by a minor subset of CTIP2+ pyramidal-tract neurons at P7 (10 ± 2%).
source: However, in contrast to the temporally stable and relatively uniform expression of FOXP2 by CT neurons in layer 6 of the postnatal SSC (Figure 1), FOXP2 was expressed by a minor subset of CTIP2+ PT neurons at P0 (34 ± 3%) and P7 (10 ± 2%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), and was almost completely absent from retrogradely labeled PT neurons in Layer 5 of SSC by P14 (4.4 ± 1.7%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: FOXP2 is almost completely absent from retrogradely labeled pyramidal-tract neurons in Layer 5 of somatosensory cortex by P14 (4.4 ± 1.7%).
source: However, in contrast to the temporally stable and relatively uniform expression of FOXP2 by CT neurons in layer 6 of the postnatal SSC (Figure 1), FOXP2 was expressed by a minor subset of CTIP2+ PT neurons at P0 (34 ± 3%) and P7 (10 ± 2%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), and was almost completely absent from retrogradely labeled PT neurons in Layer 5 of SSC by P14 (4.4 ± 1.7%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Immunohistochemistry verified the elimination of FOXP2 from tdTomato+ neurons of Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2fx/fx mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry verified the elimination of FOXP2 from tdTomato+ neurons of Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2fx/fx mice (Figure 2A, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A inset.

claim: tdTomato-expressing cell bodies remained limited to layer 6 of the cerebral cortex in Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2fx/fx mice.
source: tdTomato-expressing cell bodies remained limited to layer 6 of the cerebral cortex across genotypes, consistent with the absence of gross changes in laminar patterns due to Foxp2 deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from microscopy data.

claim: There are no overt changes in the distribution of tdTomato-labeled neurites in superficial layers of cortex in Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2fx/fx mice.
source: Confocal microscopy further revealed no overt changes in the distribution of tdTomato-labeled neurites in more superficial layers of cortex, suggesting minimal morphological rearrangement of the CT neuron population in response to Foxp2 deletion.
evidence: The claim is based on confocal microscopy observations.

claim: There is a nearly identical pattern of corticothalamic innervation across Foxp2 genotypes.
source: Inspection of tdTomato-labeled efferent axons arising from the deep layer neurons revealed a nearly identical pattern of CT innervation across Foxp2 genotypes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is normal fasciculation within the internal capsule and extensive axonal elaboration in the dorsal thalamus and thalamic reticular nuclei of Foxp2 conditional knockout mice.
source: There was normal fasciculation within the internal capsule and extensive axonal elaboration in the dorsal thalamus and thalamic reticular nuclei of Foxp2 conditional knockout mice, their heterozygous littermates and Ntsr1-cre; Rosa-tdTomato mice on a wild-type C57Bl/6J background.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations across genotypes.

claim: FOXP2 is dispensable for the typical positioning of corticothalamic neurons in layer 6 and the guidance of their axons to reach and ramify in their normal dorsal thalamic targets.
source: This suggests that FOXP2 is dispensable for the typical positioning of CT neurons in layer 6 and the guidance of their axons to reach and ramify in their normal dorsal thalamic targets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of anatomical defects observed in conditional knockout mice.

claim: The percentage of tdTomato+ corticothalamic neurons that co-express GFP is minimal and indistinguishable across Foxp2 genotypes (WT: 1.9 ± 0.4; cHET: 2.7 ± 0.1; cKO: 2 ± 0.5).
source: Unexpectedly, the percentage of GFP and tdTomato double-positive neurons was minimal and indistinguishable across genotypes (Figure 2B,C; one-way ANOVA, p=0.441; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2+/+ (WT) mean ± SEM = 1.9 ± 0.4; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/+ (cHET), mean ± SEM = 2.7 ± 0.1; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 2 ± 0.5), indicating that the exclusion of Met expression from CT neurons occurs independent of transcriptional regulation by FOXP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The exclusion of Met expression from corticothalamic neurons occurs independent of transcriptional regulation by FOXP2.
source: Unexpectedly, the percentage of GFP and tdTomato double-positive neurons was minimal and indistinguishable across genotypes (Figure 2B,C; one-way ANOVA, p=0.441; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2+/+ (WT) mean ± SEM = 1.9 ± 0.4; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/+ (cHET), mean ± SEM = 2.7 ± 0.1; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 2 ± 0.5), indicating that the exclusion of Met expression from CT neurons occurs independent of transcriptional regulation by FOXP2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of ectopic Met expression in FOXP2-deficient corticothalamic neurons.

claim: There is minimal co-expression of CCK by tdTomato+ neurons across Foxp2 genotypes (WT: 0.6 ± 0.4; cHET: 1.2 ± 0.4; cKO: 0.6 ± 0.4).
source: Despite abundant CCK expression among layer 6 neurons, there was minimal co-expression of CCK by tdTomato+ neurons across Foxp2 genotypes (Figure 2C,D; one-way ANOVA, p=0.5016; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2+/+ (WT) mean ± SEM = 0.6 ± 0.4; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/+ (cHET), mean ± SEM = 1.2 ± 0.4; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 0.6 ± 0.4), consistent with selective CCK expression by layer 6 CC neurons and exclusion from CT neurons, as previously reported (Watakabe et al., 2012; Kast et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: FOXP2 is not required for the exclusion of CCK and Met expression from corticothalamic neurons.
source: These data indicate that FOXP2 is not required for the exclusion of CCK and Met expression from CT neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of ectopic CCK and Met expression in FOXP2-deficient corticothalamic neurons.

claim: FOG2 is expressed in nearly 100% of corticothalamic neurons, independent of Foxp2 genotype (WT: 97.1 ± 0.1; cHET: 97.5 ± 0.7; cKO: 96.1 ± 0.7).
source: FOG2 immunolabeling was detected in nearly 100% of CT neurons, independent of Foxp2 genotype (Figure 2E,F; one-way ANOVA, p=0.3163; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2+/+ (WT) mean ± SEM = 97.1 ± 0.1; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/+ (cHET), mean ± SEM = 97.5 ± 0.7; Ntsr1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 96.1 ± 0.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Cre-dependent tdTomato expression in Ntsr1-cre mice begins at E17.5.
source: Expression of tdTomato was not detected until E17.5, when it was localized in a sparse population of subplate and layer 6 neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination in the Ntsr1-cre line does not begin until approximately E17.
source: Thus, cre-mediated recombination in the Ntsr1-cre line does not begin until approximately E17, well after Foxp2 expression is initiated in the cerebral cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Ferland et al., 2003), and at a developmental time point only shortly preceding the initial innervation of the thalamus by descending CT axons (Grant et al., 2012; Torii et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the timing of tdTomato expression onset and is supported by citations.

claim: Emx1-cre exhibits cre-mediated recombination in dorsal pallial progenitors beginning at E10.5.
source: To determine whether Foxp2 might play a role earlier in the development of cortical neurons, the Emx1-cre driver line was employed, which exhibits cre-mediated recombination in dorsal pallial progenitors beginning at E10.5, when they have just started to proliferate (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the Emx1-cre line.

claim: In situ hybridization revealed the selective removal of the floxed portion of the Foxp2Fx allele at E14.5.
source: In situ hybridization revealed the selective removal of the floxed portion of the Foxp2Fx allele, which encodes the DNA-binding domain, at E14.5 (Figure 3A), prior to FOXP2 protein production in the dorsal pallium (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry demonstrated the absence of FOXP2 protein in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx embryos at E16.5.
source: FOXP2 immunohistochemistry performed on sections of the E16.5 forebrain demonstrated the absence of FOXP2 protein in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx embryos at the earliest timepoint that FOXP2 could be detected in Foxp2Fx embryos (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FOG2 and CTIP2 immunohistochemistry reveals similar distributions of laminar specific markers at P0 in Foxp2Fx/Fx and Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx mice.
source: FOG2 (green) and CTIP2 (magenta) immunohistochemistry in coronal sections of the primary somatosensory cortex of Foxp2Fx/Fx and Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx mice reveals similar distributions of laminar specific markers at P0.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There are no overt differences in the thickness of cortical layers as revealed by DAPI staining at P0 or P14 in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx mice.
source: There also were no overt differences in the thickness of layers as revealed by DAPI staining at P0 or P14 (Figure 3C,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by DAPI staining data shown in Figure 3C,J.

claim: The numbers of CTIP2+/FOG2- cells in layer five are not different between genotypes at P0.
source: The numbers of CTIP2+/FOG2- cells in layer five were not different between genotypes at P0 (Figure 3E Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The numbers of FOG2+ cells in layer 6 are comparable across genotypes at P0.
source: The numbers of FOG2+ cells in layer 6 were comparable across genotypes (Figure 3F; Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.0437, Foxp2Fx, mean ± SEM = 416 ± 28; cHET, mean ± SEM = 440 ± 68; cKO, mean ± SEM = 357 ± 37; Emx1-cre, mean ± SEM = 430 ± 52), as no statistically significant pairwise differences were observed between genotypes (Dunn's Multiple Comparisons test: cKO vs. Foxp2Fx, p=0.3688; cKO vs. Emx1-cre, p=0.1353; cKO vs. cHET, p=0.0674; cHET vs. Foxp2Fx, p=0.9999; cHET vs. Emx1-cre, p=0.9999; Foxp2Fx vs. Emx1-cre, p=0.9999).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The numbers of FOG2+ layer 6 corticothalamic cells are similar in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx and Foxp2Fx/Fx littermates at P14 (Foxp2Fx/Fx: 209 ± 21; cKO: 199 ± 13).
source: Importantly, at P14, the numbers of FOG2+ layer 6 CT cells were similar in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx and Foxp2Fx/Fx littermates (Figure 3I, unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.6912 Foxp2Fx/Fx, mean ± SEM = 209 ± 21; Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 199 ± 13), as were the numbers of CTIP2+/FOG2- cells in layer 5 (unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.99; Foxp2Fx/Fx, mean ± SEM = 77 ± 14; Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 79 ± 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The numbers of CTIP2+/FOG2- cells in layer 5 are similar in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx and Foxp2Fx/Fx littermates at P14 (Foxp2Fx/Fx: 77 ± 14; cKO: 79 ± 7).
source: Importantly, at P14, the numbers of FOG2+ layer 6 CT cells were similar in Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx and Foxp2Fx/Fx littermates (Figure 3I, unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.6912 Foxp2Fx/Fx, mean ± SEM = 209 ± 21; Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 199 ± 13), as were the numbers of CTIP2+/FOG2- cells in layer 5 (unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.99; Foxp2Fx/Fx, mean ± SEM = 77 ± 14; Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 79 ± 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis.

claim: The corticofugal populations that express FOXP2 during development do not require FOXP2 for their proper specification.
source: These data demonstrate that the corticofugal populations that express FOXP2 during development do not require FOXP2 for their proper specification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal numbers of FOG2+ and CTIP2+ neurons in conditional knockout mice.

claim: The number of ppCCK+ layer 6 corticocortical cells is indistinguishable between conditional knockout and control groups at P14 (Foxp2Fx/Fx: 139 ± 7; cKO: 147 ± 9).
source: Additionally, the number of ppCCK+ layer 6 CC cells was indistinguishable between conditional knockout and control groups (Figure 3G,H. unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.5178; Foxp2Fx/Fx, mean ± SEM = 139 ± 7; Emx1-cre; Foxp2Fx/Fx (cKO), mean ± SEM = 147 ± 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The infragranular layers develop their normal complement of diverse projection neuron subtypes in normal numbers in the absence of Foxp2.
source: Thus, the infragranular layers, which contain the neurons that express FOXP2, develop their normal complement of diverse projection neuron subtypes in normal numbers in the absence of Foxp2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal numbers of different neuron subtypes in conditional knockout mice.

claim: The radial thickness of the somatosensory cortex is indistinguishable across genotypes at P14.
source: Finally, the radial thickness of the SSC was indistinguishable across genotypes at P14 (Figure 3J,K, unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.583), suggesting that FOXP2 function also is dispensable to produce a histogenically and architecturally normal SSC.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: FOXP2 function is dispensable to produce a histogenically and architecturally normal somatosensory cortex.
source: Finally, the radial thickness of the SSC was indistinguishable across genotypes at P14 (Figure 3J,K, unpaired two-tailed t-test, p=0.583), suggesting that FOXP2 function also is dispensable to produce a histogenically and architecturally normal SSC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal cortical thickness and organization in conditional knockout mice.

claim: tdTomato-labeled subcortical innervation reveals nearly identical patterns in the internal capsule, thalamus, cerebral peduncle, and pyramidal decussation across Foxp2 genotypes at P4.
source: In agreement with the results from the Ntsr1-cre; Rosa-tdTomato experiments, tdTomato-labeled subcortical innervation revealed nearly identical patterns in the internal capsule, thalamus, cerebral peduncle, and pyramidal decussation across Foxp2 genotypes at P0 (data not shown) and P4 (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Foxp2 is dispensable for proper specification of the cortical neuron subtypes that normally express FOXP2 in somatosensory cortex.
source: This result, using a genetic deletion strategy prior to cortical neurogenesis, indicates that Foxp2 is dispensable for proper specification of the cortical neuron subtypes that normally express FOXP2 in SSC, and the appropriate guidance and targeting of their efferent axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal development of FOXP2-expressing neurons in conditional knockout mice.

claim: Foxp2 is dispensable for the appropriate guidance and targeting of efferent axons from cortical neurons that normally express FOXP2.
source: This result, using a genetic deletion strategy prior to cortical neurogenesis, indicates that Foxp2 is dispensable for proper specification of the cortical neuron subtypes that normally express FOXP2 in SSC, and the appropriate guidance and targeting of their efferent axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal axon targeting patterns in conditional knockout mice.

claim: Foxp2 is not required for establishing basic developmental organization, molecular phenotypes or efferent connectivity of Foxp2-expressing neurons in somatosensory cortex of mice.
source: The current study focused on putative roles for FOXP2 in murine cortical histogenesis, using conditional mouse genetics. The results demonstrate that Foxp2 is not required for establishing basic developmental organization, molecular phenotypes or efferent connectivity of Foxp2-expressing neurons in SSC of mice.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: FOXP2 expression within the infragranular layers of the developing somatosensory cortex is present in nearly all corticothalamic neurons.
source: The connectivity and molecular phenotyping data generated here demonstrate that, in mice, FOXP2 expression within the infragranular layers of the developing SSC is present in nearly all CT neurons, excluded from most layer 6 CC neurons, and transiently expressed by a minor subset of PT neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including retrograde tracing and molecular marker analysis.

claim: FOXP2 expression within the infragranular layers of the developing somatosensory cortex is excluded from most layer 6 corticocortical neurons.
source: The connectivity and molecular phenotyping data generated here demonstrate that, in mice, FOXP2 expression within the infragranular layers of the developing SSC is present in nearly all CT neurons, excluded from most layer 6 CC neurons, and transiently expressed by a minor subset of PT neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including retrograde tracing and molecular marker analysis.

claim: FOXP2 is transiently expressed by a minor subset of pyramidal-tract neurons.
source: The connectivity and molecular phenotyping data generated here demonstrate that, in mice, FOXP2 expression within the infragranular layers of the developing SSC is present in nearly all CT neurons, excluded from most layer 6 CC neurons, and transiently expressed by a minor subset of PT neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including CTIP2 colocalization and retrograde tracing.

claim: Expression of FOXP2 by corticothalamic-type neurons is stable during postnatal development.
source: Analysis of SSC at three postnatal ages demonstrated that expression of FOXP2 by CT-type neurons is stable, whereas PT-type neurons express FOXP2 transiently, with no detectable FOXP2 expression in most PT-type neurons at P14.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data at multiple postnatal ages.

claim: Pyramidal-tract-type neurons express FOXP2 transiently during development.
source: Analysis of SSC at three postnatal ages demonstrated that expression of FOXP2 by CT-type neurons is stable, whereas PT-type neurons express FOXP2 transiently, with no detectable FOXP2 expression in most PT-type neurons at P14.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data at multiple postnatal ages.

claim: Deletion of Foxp2 does not alter expression patterns of Met or Cck in layer 6 neurons.
source: However, deletion of Foxp2 failed to alter expression patterns of Met or Cck, suggesting other transcriptional mechanisms may mediate their cell type-specific expression in infragranular layers in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data in conditional knockout mice.

claim: Other transcriptional mechanisms may mediate cell type-specific expression of Met and Cck in infragranular layers.
source: However, deletion of Foxp2 failed to alter expression patterns of Met or Cck, suggesting other transcriptional mechanisms may mediate their cell type-specific expression in infragranular layers in vivo.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the lack of effect of Foxp2 deletion on Met and Cck expression.

claim: Foxp2 is neither required for the specification of some of the unique molecular features of FOXP2+ layer 6 corticothalamic neurons, nor for the regulation of alternate cell-type molecular signatures.
source: Additionally, two important molecular features unique to FOXP2+ neurons, FOG2 and DARPP-32 expression, are unchanged following either very early or late prenatal deletion of Foxp2. Much broader molecular profiling is warranted, but the data indicate that Foxp2 is neither required for the specification of some of the unique molecular features of FOXP2+ layer 6 CT neurons, nor for the regulation of alternate cell-type molecular signatures that were predicted from previous analysis of FOXP2 transcriptional regulatory targets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of changes in molecular markers in conditional knockout mice.

claim: Foxp2 deletion does not disrupt the normal generation and migration of neurons in somatosensory cortex.
source: Using the early expressing Emx1-cre driver line (E10.5), the data show that Foxp2 deletion does not disrupt the normal generation and migration of neurons in SSC.
evidence: The claim is supported by normal lamination and cell numbers in conditional knockout mice.

claim: FOXP2 appears dispensable for the general production of cortical neurons and the specification of the specific projection populations that normally express FOXP2.
source: Thus, unlike other transcriptional regulators of cell-type identity (e.g. CTIP2, FEZF2, TBR1), for which dramatic changes in cell type numbers and projection phenotypes develop upon mutation (Arlotta et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Han et al., 2011; McKenna et al., 2011; Molyneaux et al., 2005), FOXP2 appears dispensable for the general production of cortical neurons and the specification of the specific projection populations that normally express FOXP2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of developmental defects in conditional knockout mice and is contrasted with other transcription factors.

claim: The lack of developmental defects in Nex1-cre; Foxp2Fx mice is consistent with the findings of the current study.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the absence of developmental defects recently reported in Nex1-cre; Foxp2Fx mice, in which Foxp2 is deleted from postmitotic excitatory neurons of the dorsal pallium (Medvedeva et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to another study with similar findings.

claim: Mosaic expression of Foxp2 could result in atypical interactions between neighboring FOXP2+ and FOXP2- cells.
source: The altered neurogenesis phenotype observed following IUEP mediated-knockdown could result from the removal of Foxp2 in a mosaic fashion in the dorsal pallium resulting in atypical interactions between neighboring FOXP2+ and FOXP2- cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for discrepant findings between different methodologies.

claim: Mosaic expression of mutant and wild-type alleles can influence cortical development.
source: A similar mosaic effect could explain the altered migration observed following IUEP of Foxp2 shRNA (Tsui et al., 2013). Mosaic expression of mutant and wild-type alleles can influence cortical development, shown recently in mouse models of X-linked Pcdh19 epilepsy (Pederick et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating mosaic effects in a different genetic context.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of Foxp2 results in an arrest in the radial migration of cortical neurons similar to that caused by Foxp2 shRNA knockdown.
source: Noteworthy is the finding that ectopic overexpression of Foxp2 results in a paradoxically similar arrest in the radial migration of cortical neurons caused by Foxp2 shRNA knockdown (Clovis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study showing effects of Foxp2 overexpression.

claim: Recombination of the Foxp2Fx allele does not trigger genetic compensation by other Foxp family members.
source: Additionally, it is noteworthy that, in a previous study, quantification of Foxp1 and Foxp4 transcript levels demonstrated that these genes were expressed at similar levels in WT and Foxp2 conditional knockout embryos (French et al., 2007). Thus, recombination of the Foxp2Fx allele does not necesarrily trigger genetic compensation by other Foxp family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study that measured Foxp1 and Foxp4 expression levels.

claim: Foxp2 does not play an essential role in murine somatosensory cortex neurogenesis, neuron migration, subtype specification or axonal pathfinding.
source: Although unidentified compensatory mechanisms may mask a dispensable role that Foxp2 plays in the core aspects of cortical development studied here, based on results obtained following complete genetic removal of Foxp2 function, we conclude that Foxp2 does not play an essential role in murine SSC neurogenesis, neuron migration, subtype specification or axonal pathfinding, contrary to conclusions of other studies.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, based on the lack of developmental defects in conditional knockout mice.

claim: Loss of FOXP2 function likely does not contribute to speech and language deficits through altered cortical histogenesis.
source: The results may have implications for understanding the involvement of the cerebral cortex in speech and language impairments associated with FOXP2 mutations in humans (Vargha-Khadem et al., 2005). The results suggest that loss of FOXP2 function likely does not contribute to these deficits through altered cortical histogenesis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the lack of histogenic defects in mouse models.

claim: Novel species-specific roles for Foxp2 may have been acquired in the human lineage.
source: However, it is important to note that the present studies were carried out in mice, and thus it remains possible that novel species-specific roles for Foxp2 may have been acquired in the human lineage.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging limitations of the mouse model.

claim: Conventional magnetic resonance imaging of brain structure in patients with FOXP2 mutations did not identify substantive alterations in gray and white matter structure of the cerebral cortex.
source: The normal development of cortical phenotypes in Foxp2 conditional knockout mice is consistent with conventional magnetic resonance imaging of brain structure in patients with FOXP2 mutations, which did not identify substantive alterations in gray and white matter structure of the cerebral cortex (Vargha-Khadem et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a neuroimaging study in human patients.

claim: Voxel-based morphometric analysis identified spatially restricted, minor alterations in the gray matter in perisylvian cortical areas of patients with FOXP2 mutations.
source: However, more refined analysis using voxel-based morphometric analysis identified spatially restricted, minor alterations in the gray matter in perisylvian cortical areas of patients with FOXP2 mutations (Belton et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a neuroimaging study in human patients.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination of the conditional Foxp2 allele produces a nonsense mutation that eliminates DNA-binding ability and causes near complete loss of FOXP2 protein.
source: Cre-mediated recombination of the conditional Foxp2 allele produces a nonsense mutation that eliminates DNA-binding ability and causes near complete loss of FOXP2 protein (French et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing the conditional allele.

claim: In Foxp2 constitutive knockout mice, medium spiny neurons of the striatum display decreased mEPSC frequency, decreased dendritic spine density, and increased mEPSC amplitudes.
source: Finally, in Foxp2 constitutive knockout mice, medium spiny neurons of the striatum display decreased mEPSC frequency, decreased dendritic spine density, and increased mEPSC amplitudes, whereas the macro-level organization and cell-type composition of the striatum remains intact (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing synaptic properties in Foxp2 knockout mice.

claim: The macro-level organization and cell-type composition of the striatum remains intact in Foxp2 constitutive knockout mice.

claim: Altered excitability of corticothalamic neurons could contribute to atypical activity within cortico-striato-thalamocortical loops that are important for motor control and information processing.
source: Altered excitability of CT neurons could contribute to atypical activity within cortico-striato-thalamocortical loops that are important for motor control and information processing, which could significantly alter speech related functions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for speech-related deficits.

claim: The histological organization of the somatosensory cortex is unaffected by the removal of Foxp2.
source: The demonstration that the histological organization of the somatosensory cortex is unaffected by the removal of Foxp2 warrants more detailed characterization of cortical circuit function in Foxp2 mutant mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by the anatomical and molecular data from conditional knockout mice.

claim: Human neuroimaging and animal studies have identified alterations in basal ganglia function that could contribute to clinical disorder symptoms associated with FOXP2 mutations.
source: Human neuroimaging and animal studies have identified alterations in basal ganglia function that could contribute to the clinical disorder symptoms (Vargha-Khadem et al., 1998; Belton et al., 2003; Groszer et al., 2008; French et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2016), but whether changes in cerebral cortical organization and function are critically involved in impairments associated with FOXP2 mutations is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple neuroimaging and animal studies.

claim: Whether changes in cerebral cortical organization and function are critically involved in impairments associated with FOXP2 mutations is currently unknown.

evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The winged helix transcription factor, FOXP2, has been implicated in ontogenetic processes relevant to the development of the cerebral cortex.
source: The winged helix transcription factor, FOXP2, has been implicated in ontogenetic processes relevant to the development of the cerebral cortex (Vernes et al., 2011; Chiu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2016), and some studies have directly implicated FOXP2 in cortical ontogeny (Tsui et al., 2013; Garcia-Calero et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some studies have directly implicated FOXP2 in cortical ontogeny.
source: The winged helix transcription factor, FOXP2, has been implicated in ontogenetic processes relevant to the development of the cerebral cortex (Vernes et al., 2011; Chiu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2016), and some studies have directly implicated FOXP2 in cortical ontogeny (Tsui et al., 2013; Garcia-Calero et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies specifically examining cortical development.

claim: Impairments in fundamental aspects of cortical development can lead to lifelong dysfunction of the cortex.
source: Impairments in these fundamental aspects of development can lead to lifelong dysfunction of the cortex, which is believed to contribute to core symptoms of many neurodevelopmental disorders (Rubenstein and Rakic, 2013).

claim: Foxp2 plays a more limited role in cortical development than previously thought.
source: Surprisingly, the results demonstrate that Foxp2 function is not required for many functions that it has been proposed to regulate, and therefore plays a more limited role in cortical development than previously thought.
